newsitem.title: USA: Republican warns of "phony" partisan compromise.
newsitem.headline: Republican warns of "phony" partisan compromise.

text.p: Delivering the Republican response to President Bill Clinton's State of the Union message, Representative J.C. Watts hailed Clinton's call to bipartisanship but rejected mere "feel-good" cooperation between the parties.
Watts, the only black Republican in Congress who is emerging as a party celebrity in his second congressional term, said the American people do seek bipartisanship.
But he said: "They don't want phony compromise, they don't want the kind of weak, back-scratching, go-along-to-get-along bipartisanship that makes lawmakers feel good, but gets bad results."

Watts, a conservative 39-year-old former college football star from Oklahoma, was picked for the high-profile role of following Clinton on the nation's TV screens and had been given previous prominent roles.

He delivered a stirring speech to the Republican national convention last August and has delivered party radio addresses. He devoted part of his speech on Tuesday to telling about his upbringing in Oklahoma and the importance of traditional family values.
Watts cited the president's signing of a Republican welfare reform bill and his support for a balanced federal budget as examples of "bipartisanship that works."

He applauded Clinton's interest in tax relief but said: "Working Americans need real tax relief, not just the so-called targeted tax cuts to help one group at the expense of another. We all pay too much in taxes."

Watts called on viewers to write to their members of Congress in support of a Republican-proposed balanced budget amendment to the Constitution soon to be debated in Congress, urging them to disregard dire warnings that the amendment would wreck Social Security. Clinton opposes the amendment and used the Social Security warning in Tuesday's speech.
On racial discrimination, Watts criticised "a bunch of sermons and sloganizing" by the administration and others "that defends the old assumption that government can heal the racial divide."
He said legislation had its place but could not solve racial problems alone, adding: "In fact, government sometimes rubs the wound raw, and makes the healing harder."
